title: How Many Times
mood: Aboard the enemy’s ship, Vexana asks its commander for answers, and gets more than she came for.

hero.alt: Dark planets hang in a long row in the void beside a bursting white star, pink threads of light running between them.

segs.t: Vexana leaned toward the Citadel with her staff in her fist, and the dark carried her there.
No order had sent her. She went between errands, on her own.
If the body kept the Core, its commander might know where. And its commander talked.
Up close, the Citadel’s violet storm made a low roar with no wind in it. Her robe never stirred.

The ship did not end. Each black block was as big as a district of Terrinia. She came down on the edge of one. Heat rose through her boots from the ship’s red-orange heart, glowing far down between the blocks.
Gray Enders stood along the edge, facing the storm. The cold point of the mark sat behind her breastbone, and they let her by.
Let the Will watch,
she thought.
A girl in its shape, come to see its commander.
The Citadel’s streets hung upside down. She walked them anyway, boots on the paving, towers reaching away over her head into the storm. Past their tips, more blocks hung toward her, roofs first.
Each block had come from a city. In one the stairs were too tall for any human leg. In another, torn awnings hung over empty market stalls. Nothing lived in any of them.
Then one block stopped her.

Its doors were cut for someone her height. Each stair fit her stride, and the middle of each was worn into a dip. A lamp post leaned at a corner with its glass gone. Over one shop hung a sign in letters she could almost read.
She stood under the sign and tried. The letters would not come.
“You came looking for something.”
Obsidia waited at the far end of the street, a hand’s width above the paving. Vexana had not heard her come.
Of course. It is her ship.
She already holds the star over me,
Vexana thought.
Asking cannot cost me more.
“The Core,” she said.
Obsidia did not answer that. Her eyes went once to Vexana’s right sleeve, and away. “Walk.”
Vexana walked. Far off, beyond the storm, hung the crack of human sky.
“It showed me the end,” she said. “It said it was no judgment.”
“It was not. The judging was done before it came.”
“By whom?”
Obsidia pointed at the crack. “By your world.”
Vexana looked. Under that sky she had sat by a shady tree, Guinevere’s head in her lap.
That sky judged us?
“Chang’e taught us a rule,” said Vexana. “A planet that holds Balance. A people grown too strong. Who gave a planet the right?”
“The universe. Its own will is Balance, and has been since its first moment, out of the chaos before it.”
“Balance. I know the word.”
“Then learn the rest. Some galaxies grow wills of their own and keep the balance on its behalf. So do some worlds in them. Yours grew one long after it was born.”
“A planet with a will.”
“You live on one. It looked at its humans and found them too prosperous. So it sent for us.”
“Prosperous? We live under a dome.”
“Not when it judged. Before we came this time, your kind had filled this world with cities.”
“This time?”
Obsidia drifted on.
Vexana heard the vision’s voice again.
This is no judgment.
It was reading me a verdict,
she thought.
Someone else had passed it.
“It hates us,” she said.
“No. Flesh does not hate a splinter. It pushes it out.”
Her thumb pressed the brass collar on her staff.
Her father on the wall before dawn, oiling the guns so the street behind him could sleep. One lit window across the city, long past midnight.
That is what it weighed,
she thought.
And found too much.
She kept her stride. The heat came up through her boots.
No,
she thought, and again,
no.
They walked the length of a block without a word.
“And the voice in my head,” said Vexana at last. “Is it this world’s mind, or yours?”
“Not mine. It is one being, the Will of the Planet. It serves every world that holds Balance. On each one it is that world’s will, made able to move.”
“Where did it come from?”
Obsidia looked up into the storm. “Before me. The oldest pulses carry one memory: a Twilight Orb, a sphere of light, bursting open. I think the Will was born of it. I cannot ask.”
“And you? What are you to it?”
“I am its Will, the ender of civilizations,” said Obsidia.
“Its Will,” said Vexana. “Then why cut its healing short?”
Obsidia stopped drifting.
“You listen well,” she said. Her silver-pink weapon turned in the air beside her until its point faced Vexana. Then it turned away.
“My father fought your kind,” said Vexana. “The children on our street never did.”
“Every civilization tries to transcend its own host,” said Obsidia.
“Host.”
“The planet. A people that outgrows its host uses it up, then reaches for other worlds. Left alone, it leaves a dead world. A purge leaves the host alive, to begin again.”
“And a people who stay small?”
Obsidia’s claw moved toward the dark. “Some worlds cut their own people down from within, to stay too small for their world to send for us. They pay for it every day.”
The block ended at an edge. Vexana looked over.

Beneath the foundations ran one gray cord. Every block she had walked hung from it, and every block in sight. It was the only thing aboard that moved like flesh. It swelled and sank, slow, as if it breathed.
“How does it go?” said Vexana. “The purge.”
“As it always goes. A host finds its people too prosperous. The Will stirs. The body rises in the void, and the nest fills.”
“The nest. Where is it?”
“Where the body grows new Enders and keeps them in rows until they are sent.”
The rows I see from the hollow,
Vexana thought. She had never walked among them. One more place to search.
“Then its commander is called up out of the long sleep, and small doors open near the people. Enders come through.”
“The Catastrophe,” said Vexana.
“Your people’s name for it. We die in numbers, and the Will goes dark for a while. Then it stirs again and sends more.”
The lulls,
Vexana thought.

“If a people fight until the purge stalls, the body opens a great door and comes down itself. Its commander follows with her ship, when she chooses. Then their civilization ends, and all returns to chaos. We sleep, and the host begins again.”
All returns to chaos.
The voice in the vision had said those words too.
“We have been winning,” said Vexana.

“You had won fights before. Never like that one: so many of us broken at once, by your hands. At a breach in your dome, some weeks before you came here.” Obsidia watched her face. “That is the step that brings the body down.”

Vexana remembered the breach. The torn shell of the dome in the Northeastern sector. Guinevere below her, fists up, her drones circling. Whatever reached for Guinevere’s back, Vexana’s magic hit first.
They had held their end until the last Ender fell. The city had won.
The crack of sky had already been there when the dark took her.
It opened after we won,
she thought.
We did that. I did.
“Does it weigh on you,” said Obsidia, “what your victory bought?”
Vexana walked on. “Tell me the rest.”
Their walk had come round. They were back in the street with the doors her height.
“Whose street is this?” said Vexana.
“A people much like yours. I helped end them.”
“Where?”
Obsidia looked at the crack. “Under that sky.”
Before we came this time.
Vexana looked down at the worn dip in the nearest stair.
Obsidia let her look. “How many times do you think humanity has walked the same path?”
Vexana set her boot in the dip. It fit.
She thought of the steep wall stair at home, its steps worn into dips like this one by Shield boots. Her legs had given out halfway up it once, and her father had carried her the rest.
She did not answer.
“And the ones who lived?” she said at last.

“A purge ends a civilization, not every life. The few left kept no cities and no records. Their children built again and remembered nothing.” Obsidia touched the bent lamp post. “This street is a piece of their city.”
“That’s your story,” said Vexana.
“It is the only one that was there.”
Vexana looked up at the sign she could not read.
If it is true...
“You keep their lamp posts,” she said.
“The body grew the living part for me when I woke. The rest I built from what I ended.”
Terrinia next,

Vexana thought. In her mind the Academy’s tower hung among these blocks, upside down, its white-cyan beam out. Beside it hung the courtyard billboard, GUINEVERE and VEXANA in big letters. One day someone would stand under it and try to read them. The letters would not come.
“And you will hang us here,” she said.
Her thumb pressed the brass collar again, hard.

Obsidia let it stand. “Your world’s own life began under falling stones. For ages they struck it, and what they carried became its first living things.” She opened her hand, palm down, over the street. “Destruction is merely the beginning of a new cycle.”
“Why tell me any of this?”
“You asked. And I wished to see what a human does with it.”
“And the Core?”
Obsidia lifted her hand. At the end of the street a whole block ground against its neighbor and swung aside. Open dark showed where it had been.
“Another time.”
Her power reaches the whole ship,
Vexana thought. She had come for the Core.
She walked back out through the hanging streets.
It does not hate us. So it cannot be begged.
Her grip tightened on the staff.
Then it has to be broken.
Behind her the block ground back into place. Between the streets, in the dark, the gray cord breathed on.
